title: Streaming service content operations
transcript:
Priya (Head of Content Operations, Lumen Streaming): Thanks for making time. Quick background: we run a regional streaming service, about 4,000 titles, and every title needs artwork and metadata localised into six languages before it goes live.

Marco (Solutions Engineer): Great. Walk me through how that works today.

Priya: It's a mess, honestly. Editors get a spreadsheet from licensing, they email the artwork team, the artwork team resizes images by hand for each device, and then someone copies everything into our CMS. A new title takes about nine working days to go live. Our target is three.

Marco: Where does the time go?

Priya: Mostly waiting. Artwork requests sit in a shared inbox. And localisation vendors send back files in different formats.

Daniel (Engineering Lead): I'd add that the CMS is a custom system. It has a REST API but the documentation is out of date. We can't replace it this year, that's a hard constraint.

Marco: Understood, so we integrate with it rather than replace it. What volume are we talking about?

Priya: Around 150 new titles a month, plus roughly 400 metadata corrections.

Daniel: Also, anything that touches subtitles has to keep a full audit trail. Our licensors audit us twice a year.

Priya: And honestly I'd love a dashboard where I can see which titles are stuck and why. Right now I find out when someone shouts at me.

Marco: Is there a deadline?

Priya: We relaunch in the first quarter. Daniel thinks that's too ambitious.

Daniel: I think it's tight, yes. I'd rather start with artwork and metadata, and leave subtitles for a second phase.

Priya: I disagree. Subtitles are where the delays are worst. But fine, let's talk about it.

Marco: We'll come back to phasing. Last thing, who approves final output?

Priya: Always a human editor. We will not publish anything automatically.

open_questions.question: Which device image dimensions and formats are required for automated resizing?
open_questions.why_it_matters: To design the image processing pipeline that meets all playback devices.

open_questions.question: What specific file formats do localisation vendors currently deliver?
open_questions.why_it_matters: To ensure the system can ingest and normalize all incoming localisation assets.

open_questions.question: What details must be captured in the subtitle audit trail?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Compliance with bi‑annual licensor audits requires a complete and searchable audit log.

open_questions.question: What is the exact go‑live date for the Q1 relaunch?
open_questions.why_it_matters: To assess feasibility of the three‑day target and plan the phased rollout.

open_questions.why_it_matters: To design a monitoring view that surfaces stuck titles and root causes effectively.

risks.risk: The Q1 relaunch deadline may be unrealistic given current process bottlenecks.
Disagreement on phasing (Priya wants subtitles early, Daniel prefers to defer) could cause scope creep or delays.

assumptions: The custom CMS REST API is functional despite outdated documentation.
The volume of 150 new titles and 400 metadata corrections per month will remain roughly constant during implementation.

components.name: CMS Integration Service
components.responsibility: Orchestrates title lifecycle, calls custom CMS REST API, records audit events, and routes data to downstream services.
components.tech: Node.js + Express, hosted on managed container service
components.size_rationale: Requires API work, data mapping, and audit logging but no complex UI.

components.name: Managed Image Resizing Service
components.responsibility: Automatically generates all required device image sizes from source artwork.
components.tech: Vendor‑neutral managed image‑processing API (e.g., Cloudinary, Imgix)

components.name: Localization Ingestion Engine
components.responsibility: Parses vendor subtitle/localisation files, normalises them, stores them, and emits audit records.
components.tech: Python FastAPI service with pluggable file‑format adapters
components.size_rationale: Needs format parsers and validation logic plus audit hooks.

components.name: Workflow Automation Platform
components.responsibility: Provides a tracked, email‑intake workflow replacing the shared‑inbox request process, enforces human‑editor approval step.
components.tech: Vendor‑neutral workflow SaaS with REST/webhook connectors
components.size_rationale: Low‑code SaaS setup; integration points to C1, C2, C3.

components.name: Operations Dashboard
components.responsibility: Shows titles in each workflow stage, highlights stuck items and reasons, pulls data from integration service and audit store.
components.tech: React single‑page app + managed GraphQL layer
components.size_rationale: Simple UI with read‑only queries; connects to existing data sources.

components.name: Audit Log Store
components.responsibility: Immutable store of all subtitle processing actions and approval decisions for compliance.
components.tech: Managed NoSQL document store (e.g., DynamoDB, Firestore)

integrations.risk: Medium – custom CMS version changes could break contracts

tradeoffs.alternative: Build custom CMS connector from scratch
tradeoffs.reason: Integration is limited to a single REST API; building gives precise control and avoids SaaS licensing.
Image resizing is a well‑solved problem; a managed service reduces ops overhead and scales instantly.
Speed to market and built‑in tracking outweigh the modest cost; custom code would be larger (L) and riskier.

tradeoffs.alternative: Store audit logs in relational DB
tradeoffs.reason: Audit entries are append‑only and schema‑flexible; NoSQL offers cheaper storage and easier scaling.
